sentences.text: The known skull of Abelisaurus could be estimated to be over 85 cm long, with recent estimates suggesting a length of about 86 cm despite missing pieces.
The only fossil remains are of a partial skull lacking the mandible, which is incomplete especially on the right side.
The premaxilla of Abelisaurus bore four small teeth, while the maxilla behind it held at least seven, possibly up to thirteen, larger teeth.
Abelisaurus was a carnivorous dinosaur with two small rough crests on its head, but these were not as well-defined as those found in other members of its family.
Abelisaurus had a proportionally longer preorbital opening than tyrannosaurs or other Jurassic and Cretaceous dinosaurs.
The squamosal bone projecting backward with a ventrally directed quadrate jugal process places Abelisaurus with ceratosaurians rather than tyrannosaurs.
Abelisaurus had a prominent interorbital region where the lacrimal and postorbital bones contacted to form a projection on the orbit.
The high orbital foramen combined with the previously noted formation resulted in a circumference that was barely open ventrally.
The horizontal ramus of the maxilla was thick to accommodate laterally flattened teeth.
Abelisaurus was a bipedal carnivore estimated to reach about 7.4 meters in length, though this size is uncertain due to the incompleteness of the fossil record.
Although no crests or horns are present on the skull like in other found abelisaurids such as Carnotaurus, it is presumed they existed, likely made of keratin and thus not fossilized.
The genus and type species Abelisaurus comahuensis were named and described by José Bonaparte and Fernando Emilio Novas in 1985.
The generic name honors Roberto Abel, who discovered the type specimen and was the former director of the provincial Museum of Cipolletti in Argentina.
The holotype fossil MC 11098 was uncovered in 1983 at the Lago Pellegrini quarries in Argentina.
Roberto Abel discovered the remains of Abelisaurus in 1983.

José Fernando Bonaparte and Fernando Novas named the genus Abelisaurus in 1985 after its discoverer and named the species comahuensis after the Comahue region of Patagonia, Argentina, where it was found.
The holotype specimen MC 11078 was unearthed in 1983 at the "Cantera de la Pala Mecánica" site near Lago Pellegrini, which Abel had explored since 1975.
Only one fossil occurrence of Abelisaurus has been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul proposed that Abelisaurus hunted titanosaurian sauropods like Antarctosaurus and Neuquensaurus.
It is presumed that, like tyrannosaurs, abelisaurids were the apex predators of their ecosystem.
In 2010, Paul proposed that Abelisaurus hunted titanosaurid sauropods.
Bonaparte and Novas placed Abelisaurus in the family Abelisauridae in 1985, initially considering it a member of the Carnosauria.
Subsequent research showed that abelisaurids, including Abelisaurus, belong to the Neoceratosauria rather than the modern sense of Carnosauria.
Bonaparte and Novas placed Abelisaurus in its own new family, Abelisauridae, in 1985 within Carnosauria.

Many other abelisaurids have very complete specimens like Aucasaurus, Carnotaurus, and Majungasaurus; thanks to these, it was demonstrated that abelisaurids do not belong to Carnosauria in a modern sense, but instead belong to Neoceratosauria.
In 2022, Agnolín et al. placed Abelisaurus within Carnotaurinae in the clade Brachyrostra, forming a clade together with Aucasaurus.
Abelisaurus belongs to the subfamily Abelisaurinae.
Abelisaurus lived during the early Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous Period, approximately 83 to 80 million years ago.
The formation containing Abelisaurus remains has been dated to the early Campanian, late Cretaceous, between 83 and 80 million years ago.
The Anacleto Formation consists mainly of violet and dark red clay and mud of fluvial origin.
Abelisaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether Abelisaurus might actually be a carcharodontosaurid, though this hypothesis is considered unlikely by most researchers.
Some scientists consider Abelisaurus a basal abelisaurid outside the subfamily of carnotaurines, while other scientists disagree with this stance.
